text: Taught separately, incident, problem, and change management can sound like three unrelated jobs run by three unrelated teams. In a real service desk they're one continuous loop, and the handoff points between them matter as much as understanding each practice alone. Knowing where one practice's responsibility ends and the next begins is what keeps an organization from sitting on a recurring problem forever, or changing production systems with no real risk evaluation.

The loop starts where incident management left off: something breaks, gets logged, categorized, prioritized, and resolved — ideally fast, possibly with a workaround. If the incident is a genuine one-off that never recurs, the story ends right there, and most incidents do end there. The loop only continues when something is wrong in a deeper sense — it keeps coming back, or the cause still isn't understood even though the symptom got fixed.

When the same failure recurs, or shows up once with real severity, problem management picks up exactly where incident management left off. Problem identification flags the pattern, problem control investigates and finds root cause, and if a permanent fix isn't ready, it becomes a known error with a documented workaround incident management can reuse next time. Incident management keeps restoring service on each occurrence while problem management works the deeper cause in parallel.

Here's the critical constraint: problem management can diagnose a cause perfectly and still have zero authority to fix it. If the permanent fix means altering a configuration item — a setting, code, a network rule, a schema — that's officially a change, and it must go through change enablement like any other. A known error's fix typically becomes a normal change, assessed and scheduled. If it's actively driving a major incident, the fix might instead run as an emergency change — authorized fast, but genuinely authorized.

Once the change is implemented successfully, the known error closes, the problem record closes, and — the whole point of the loop — the incidents that cause used to produce stop happening. That's the real value of running all three practices as one connected system: incident management kept the business running, problem management made sure the cause never stayed a mystery, and change enablement made sure the fix went in safely instead of creating a new incident.
